title: The implied cost of capital: A new approach

models.sample_description: NYSE, Amex, and Nasdaq common shares with CRSP share codes 10 or 11 (excluding ADRs, closed-end funds, and REITs) at the CRSP/Compustat intersection. For each forecast origin year t from 1968 to 2008, the authors estimate pooled regressions on the preceding ten years and forecast earnings at horizons τ=1,…,5 using year-t inputs. Firms need nonmissing year-t predictors to receive forecasts. The paper does not report the exact observation count for any year/horizon training fit.
models.method_details: The authors identify pooled cross-sectional regressions but do not name the underlying estimator. Do not infer OLS from the linear equation. Each year’s fit uses the previous ten years; the paper reports time-series averages of the annual coefficients and Newey–West t-statistics for those annual coefficient estimates.
models.equation_text: E_{i,t+τ} = α_0 + α_1 A_{i,t} + α_2 D_{i,t} + α_3 DD_{i,t} + α_4 E_{i,t} + α_5 Neg E_{i,t} + α_6 AC_{i,t} + ε_{i,t+τ}, where τ=1,…,5.

fixed_effects.details: The paper does not report fixed-effect dimensions for this forecasting fit.

standard_errors.details: Table 1 reports Newey–West t-statistics for the time-series average coefficients, applying the Newey–West procedure to annual coefficient estimates. This describes inference on the reported average coefficients; the fitted annual models supply forecast coefficients.

estimation_procedure.description: For each forecast origin year t from 1968 through 2008, estimate pooled cross-sectional fits using the preceding ten years of data. Fit the horizon-specific earnings outcomes for τ=1,…,5; use the year-t explanatory variables to generate strictly out-of-sample forecasts. The table reports yearly coefficient averages; horizons four and five are estimated but not tabulated.

For each firm i and each year t in our sample, we compute earnings forecasts for up to five years into the future by multiplying the independent variables as of year t with the coefficients from the pooled regression estimated using the previous ten years of data.

sample_extraction.data_section_full_text:
2.1. Data and sample selection

Our sample includes all NYSE, Amex, and Nasdaq listed securities with sharecodes 10 or 11 (i.e., excluding ADRs,
closed-end funds, and REITs) that are at the intersection of the CRSP monthly returns file from July 1963 to June 2009 and
the Compustat fundamentals annual file from 1963 to 2009. Our results are robust to excluding utilities and financials
from the analysis. We use the following variable definitions. Earnings is income before extraordinary items from
Compustat. Book equity is Compustat stockholder’s equity. Total assets and dividends are also from Compustat. Prior to
1988, accruals are calculated using the balance sheet method as the change in non-cash current assets less the change in
current liabilities excluding the change in short-term debt and the change in taxes payable minus depreciation and
amortization expense. Starting in 1988, we use the cash flow statement method to calculate accruals as the difference
between earnings and cash flows from operations. <sup>6</sup> We also obtain consensus analyst forecasts and the corresponding
actual earnings from the IBES summary files.

2.2. Cross-sectional earnings model


To forecast earnings of individual firms, we use a model that is based on an extension and variation of the
cross-sectional profitability models in Fama and French (2000, 2006), Hou and Robinson (2006), and Hou and
van Dijk (2011). Previous studies on model-based earnings forecasts (e.g., Brown and Rozeff, 1978; Fried and Givoly, 1982;


5 A recent paper by Bradshaw et al. (2011) shows that analysts’ superiority over time-series forecasts is negligible for smaller and younger firms, and
over longer horizons.

6 See Hribar and Collins (2002) for details. Our results are robust to using the balance sheet method for the entire sample period.

K. Hou et al. / Journal of Accounting and Economics 53 (2012) 504–526 507


Brown et al., 1987; O’Brien, 1988) tend to focus on time-series models fit separately to individual firms. To enhance power,
empirical tests are usually restricted to firms with long earnings histories. This data requirement introduces survivorship
bias to the tests. In addition, estimates based on these individual time-series models are not very precise. An important
advantage of our cross-sectional approach is that it provides statistical power without imposing strict survivorship
requirements.

Specifically, for each year between 1968 and 2008, we estimate the following pooled cross-sectional regressions using
the previous ten years of data:


Ei,t þ t 1⁄4 a0 þa1Ai,t þa2Di,t þa3DDi,t þa4Ei,t þa5NegEi,t þa6ACi,t þei,t þ t, ð1Þ


where Ei,t þ t denotes the earnings of firm i in year tþt (t 1⁄41 to 5), Ai,t is the total assets, Di,t is the dividend payment, DDi,t is
a dummy variable that equals 1 for dividend payers and 0 otherwise, Neg Ei,t is a dummy variable that equals 1 for firms
with negative earnings and 0 otherwise, and ACi,t is accruals. All explanatory variables are measured as of year t.

The main difference between Eq. (1) and the cross-sectional models used in prior studies (e.g., Fama and French, 2000) is
that we use Eq. (1) to forecast dollar earnings while previous papers use cross-sectional models to forecast profitability
(earnings scaled by total assets). We focus on dollar earnings to make our forecasts comparable with analysts’ forecasts. In
addition, the ICC literature (e.g., Gebhardt et al., 2001) exclusively uses dollar earnings forecasts to estimate the ICC. That said,
we are concerned about potentially overweighting firms with extreme dollar earnings in estimating Eq. (1). <sup>7</sup> To address this
concern, we winsorize earnings and other level variables each year at the 1st and 99th percentiles (observations beyond the
extreme percentiles are set to equal to the values at those percentiles). We also carry out robustness checks in Section 6 by
scaling earnings (and the other level variables in Eq. (1)) using lagged total assets and find similar results.

For each firm i and each year t in our sample, we compute earnings forecasts for up to five years into the future by
multiplying the independent variables as of year t with the coefficients from the pooled regression estimated using the
previous ten years of data. This is to ensure that our earnings forecasts are strictly out of sample (that is, all information
that is required to forecast earnings for years tþ1 through tþ5 is available in year t). In addition, we only require a firm to
have non-missing values for the independent variables in year t to estimate its earnings forecasts. As a result, the
survivorship bias is kept to a minimum.
